name: Leydig cell tumour of the testis
aliases: interstitial cell tumour of the testis

clinicalPearls: Leydig cell tumour is the commonest sex cord-stromal tumour of the testis and most are benign, though a minority behave malignantly, particularly in adults
It can be hormonally active, secreting testosterone or oestrogen, so presentation varies by age
In prepubertal boys androgen excess may cause isosexual precocious puberty, while oestrogen excess can cause gynaecomastia
In adults it may present as a painless testicular mass, with gynaecomastia, reduced libido, or infertility from hormonal effects
Germ cell tumour markers (AFP, beta-hCG) are normal, and hormone profiling (testosterone, oestradiol, and relevant pituitary hormones) helps characterise a functioning tumour
Small, clearly benign-appearing lesions may be amenable to testis-sparing surgery, whereas radical inguinal orchidectomy is used when malignancy is suspected or organ preservation is not feasible
Features suggesting malignant potential include larger size, vascular invasion, necrosis, increased mitoses, and infiltrative margins, prompting staging and closer follow-up
reference.pathophysiology: Leydig cell tumours arise from the interstitial Leydig cells that normally produce testosterone under luteinising hormone stimulation. Neoplastic Leydig cells may retain steroidogenic activity and secrete androgens or, through peripheral or intratumoral aromatisation, oestrogens, producing the endocrine syndromes seen clinically. Excess oestrogen can suppress the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis and impair spermatogenesis, contributing to gynaecomastia and infertility. Most tumours are benign, but a subset shows histological features associated with metastatic behaviour, chiefly in adults.
additionalDifferentials: Germ cell tumour of the testis
Testicular adrenal rest tumour in congenital adrenal hyperplasia
additionalInvestigations: Scrotal ultrasound to localise and characterise the intratesticular lesion
Serum AFP and beta-hCG (normal) to exclude a germ cell tumour
Hormonal profile including testosterone, oestradiol, LH, and FSH
Assessment to exclude testicular adrenal rest tumour when congenital adrenal hyperplasia is possible
CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis when malignancy is suspected
Histological review of resection margins and malignancy-associated features
redFlags: Large or rapidly growing tumour with features suggesting malignancy
Evidence of retroperitoneal or distant metastases on staging
Rapidly progressive precocious puberty in a boy
Marked hormonal disturbance with new gynaecomastia in an adult
reference.prognosis: The majority of Leydig cell tumours are benign and cured by surgical excision, with resolution or improvement of hormonal effects; malignant Leydig cell tumours, more frequent in adults, respond poorly to chemotherapy and radiotherapy and carry a guarded prognosis once metastatic.
pitfalls: Assuming a hormonally active mass is benign without assessing malignancy-associated histological features
Overlooking bilateral testicular adrenal rest tumours in congenital adrenal hyperplasia and mistaking them for neoplasm
Proceeding to orchidectomy for a small benign lesion where testis-sparing surgery was feasible
Failing to investigate gynaecomastia or precocious puberty as a clue to a functioning tumour
references: WHO Classification of Tumours: Urinary and Male Genital Tumours
